entries.content:
On the morning of Monday, July 20, as the monsoon session of India’s parliament opened, tens of thousands of protesters surged down the radial streets leading to the heart of official New Delhi. Most of them were young people marching in response to a call issued by Sonam Wangchuk, a well-known climate activist, to bring their demands for education reform directly to lawmakers and leaders of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Police met them with batons and tear gas. More than a hundred were treated for fractures and other injuries at area hospitals. Parliament’s first day in session was dominated by opposition lawmakers’ blistering criticisms of the government’s response.

Two days earlier, Delhi police officers had descended on Jantar Mantar, the eighteenth-century astronomical observatory and frequent site of protests in the nation’s capital, where Wangchuk had been on an indefinite hunger strike since June 28. His fast was in support of a swiftly growing youth movement called the “Cockroach Janta Party,” which demanded that the education minister resign in the aftermath of the government’s controversial decision to cancel medical college examinations for more than two million students. (The movement sardonically took its name from the chief justice of India’s remarks in May comparing unemployed youths to “cockroaches.”) Claiming to act on a court order, the police pushed aside the young protesters attending to the visibly weakened Wangchuk, wrapped him in a white bedsheet, and hustled him into a waiting ambulance and off to a nearby hospital.

At first glance, the man at the center of this drama—a fifty-nine-year-old engineer from the Himalayan region of Ladakh—seems an unlikely leader for a Gen Z movement that has rapidly emerged to pose one of the biggest challenges Prime Minister Narendra Modi has yet faced during his twelve years in office. But Wangchuk’s entire career has been building toward this moment: he was propelled into public life, as a young man, by his own frustration with a broken education system and the ways in which it stymied an entire generation’s possibilities. “I have not chosen this issue today,” he explained to a reporter on July 15. “I chose this issue forty years ago when I decided to work in the field of education.” His fast was only the most recent in a series of efforts Wangchuk has made in recent years, drawing on the satyagraha methods of Mahatma Gandhi, to make the nation’s leaders and his fellow citizens attend to the precarity of India’s two most precious resources: its climate and its youth.

Before he became one of India’s most prominent activists, Wangchuk was heralded as one of its most innovative educators. In 2001 The Week magazine named him “Man of the Year” for spearheading reforms to his region’s deeply flawed education system, an initiative that led to his serving on India’s national governing council on education. A trained mechanical engineer and longstanding evangelist for renewable energy, he has—often working alongside alumni of student training programs he founded—designed and built energy-efficient earthen school buildings, devised siphon systems for draining hazardous high-altitude glacial lakes, and created solar-heated army tents and facilities to keep soldiers warm through the Himalayan winter. (I devoted a chapter of my 2015 book Fire and Ice to chronicling his indefatigable efforts to harness Ladakh’s abundant sunshine.) His elegant “ice stupas”—vertical artificial glaciers that store meltwater for farmers’ use—have spread across the Himalayas and even to the Andes and the Alps. By the end of the decade he had even become a figure in popular culture, inspiring the fearless protagonist—played by the superstar Aamir Khan—of the 2009 Bollywood hit 3 Idiots, for several years the highest-grossing film in the history of Hindi cinema.

Not long ago BJP leaders held up Wangchuk’s work as cause for national pride. In 2018, when Wangchuk won the Ramon Magsaysay Award, often described as “Asia’s Nobel Prize,” a top BJP official called him a “hero of hope” for his “outstanding contribution in harnessing nature, culture and education for community progress.” And yet over the past several years the party has come to view him with increasing suspicion.

During that time Wangchuk has leveraged his renown toward two objectives: getting the world to notice the catastrophic ongoing meltdown of the Himalayas’ snow and ice, and pressuring India’s leaders to grant constitutional protections and meaningful autonomy to Ladakh, a high-altitude region of about 300,000 people in the country’s far north that had until 2019 been part of the state of Jammu and Kashmir. That year Prime Minister Narendra Modi dissolved the state, revoked the article of the Indian constitution that had granted special protections to its inhabitants, and made Ladakh into a “union territory” to be administered directly from New Delhi. Ever since, the BJP-led government has tightened its control over Ladakh, siphoning power away from its elected district councils. In 2019 and 2020 BJP leaders made election-year pledges to grant Ladakhis self-governance powers and more formal local control over their lands and resources by granting them special protections under the constitution’s “Sixth Schedule,” a provision which has been used to devolve many powers to certain tribal areas in the northeast. But for years Modi’s administration refused to follow through on these promises and dragged out negotiations with leaders of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), the two organizations that have, to a remarkable extent, unified the region’s Buddhists and Muslims around the twin causes of securing statehood and tribal status.

Advertisement

Wangchuk’s political and climate-related goals are, he has stressed, inextricably linked. Without constitutional safeguards, “Ladakhis themselves could be completely excluded from decision-making around land use in their own land,” he told me when I interviewed him halfway through an earlier, twenty-one-day hunger strike he undertook in March 2024. Many fear the joint onslaught of climate change-driven glacier loss and unchecked resource extraction by outside actors. “There simply won’t be enough water in our high-altitude desert to support these new demands,” Wangchuk said. “Every drop here is important.”

Ten months ago Wangchuk’s years-long campaign to win these protections put him at the center of a different media and political firestorm. On September 24, 2025, he was two weeks into a planned thirty-five-day fast, along with fourteen others, in Leh, the region’s largest city. When two participants fell ill and were transported to the hospital, hundreds of young Ladakhis surged into surrounding streets and unleashed pent-up anger, setting fire to police cars and a local BJP office. Security forces fired on the crowds, killing four people—including an Indian army veteran—and injuring more than ninety. That evening Wangchuk called off the fast and made an urgent plea for peace, reminding protesters of their shared commitment to the path of nonviolent resistance. He declared it “one of the saddest days in my life.”

Two days later authorities detained Wangchuk under the draconian National Security Act, which allows the central government to hold individuals for up to twelve months without trial to prevent them from acting in a manner “prejudicial to the defence of India.” He was flown to Rajasthan and held in the high-security Jodhpur Central Jail, alongside organized crime kingpins. There he remained until March 14, just days before India’s highest court was to hold its final hearing on his imprisonment, when the home ministry—perhaps sensing that the justices would issue an embarrassing ruling in his favor—suddenly announced his release.

For those familiar with Wangchuk’s career, the charges leveled against him were shocking. Officials from the BJP branded him “chief provocateur” of the unrest in Leh. Their online allies took to social media to label him “anti-national.” In front of the Supreme Court, Wangchuk’s attorney had laid out extensive evidence showing that his detention was improper, both procedurally and on its merits. In response the government submitted AI-produced translations of a speech he had given before the riots unfolded, and accused Wangchuk of whipping up Ladakh’s youth by invoking the Gen Z revolts that had recently ousted corrupt leaders in Nepal and Bangladesh. Recordings make it clear that Wangchuk was doing precisely the opposite. In response to another speaker’s mention of those revolutions in neighboring countries, he had exhorted Ladakhis to stick to the Gandhian path instead. “I was among the speakers following, and said, ‘Somebody mentioned Nepal and Bangladesh, but that’s something we shouldn’t do in Ladakh, we should have a peaceful resolution without any violence and set an example for the world,’” he told me.

The government’s charges against Wangchuk are all the more telling in light of the protests that have erupted since—a tacit acknowledgement of its own fears, and of the potency of young Indians’ frustrations. Wangchuk often contends that his advocacy for climate protections and for Ladakh’s autonomy follow directly from his work to build cultural confidence and a sense of agency among young people across the region and throughout India. “We don’t have to repeat the mistakes made by previous powers,” he once told me. The conviction underpinning much of his work is that, if India’s decision-makers—its urban elites, corporate CEOs, university leaders, bureaucrats, chief ministers, and so on—were to tap into the ingenuity, creativity, and local knowledge of its diverse citizenry instead of following the high-consuming, high-emitting groove carved out by the Global North, they could at once do more to answer the despair of the country’s 750 million young people under the age of thirty and help show the world what a climate-conscious development path could look like.

Advertisement

The BJP’s leaders seem to view Wangchuk, warily, as a budding politician—perhaps following in the footsteps of his father, an influential political leader and minister in the Jammu and Kashmir government of the 1970s and 1980s. In the midst of Wangchuk’s fast in New Delhi, Indian media outlets resurfaced an episode from 1984, when his father undertook his own fast to demand “scheduled tribe” status for the people of Ladakh. He broke it when Prime Minister Indira Gandhi flew to Leh and offered him a glass of juice.

But as Wangchuk’s efforts to link various crises demonstrate, he is, first and foremost, a teacher. His own earliest teacher was his mother, who schooled him in the Ladakhi language at their home in Uleytokpo, a village on the banks of the Indus River that’s famed for its abundant apricot trees. He first experienced formal education as a form of abuse: at age nine he was enrolled in a school in Srinagar, where his teachers mocked him and called him a “donkey” because he couldn’t understand the orders and questions they fired at him in Urdu. He was afraid to speak up in class. (Today he’s a polyglot, fluent in seven languages.) It wasn’t until he encountered a sympathetic teacher who saw his potential, after begging his parents to let him attend a government school in New Delhi, that he was awakened to his own intellectual abilities. With newfound confidence, he earned his engineering degree from a university in Kashmir.

He began tutoring bright students who nevertheless kept failing the all-important tenth class board exam, a gateway to advancement in India. (More than 90 percent of Ladakhi students failed at the time.) Wangchuk went on to cofound, along with his brother and several friends, the Students’ Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh (SECMOL). The organization published textbooks in Ladakhi, hosted teacher trainings, and set up village education committees to hold absentee teachers and negligent administrators accountable. It sparked renewed pride in the ecologically balanced agricultural and pastoral systems that Ladakhis had perfected through centuries of living in a harsh, water-scarce environment.

In the 1990s SECMOL launched a project called Operation New Hope to reform the education system. In many rural schools, when they bothered to show up for work, teachers had students parrot back passages from textbooks about elephants and trains and other things they had never seen, in Hindi and Urdu, languages that the students barely understood. “It is what you would design for your enemy, not for your nation’s future citizens,” Wangchuk once told me. The local government adopted the group’s grassroots reforms as its own.1

In 2017 Wangchuk realized his long-held dream of creating a higher education institution where students could learn practical problem-solving skills in fields such as renewable energy, green building, water conservation, ecologically minded agriculture, and ecotourism.2 This alternative university, Himalayan Institute of Alternatives, Ladakh (HIAL), has thrived, attracting students from across India and the Himalaya-Hindu Kush, and equipping them to launch or work for ventures that address societal needs in their own regions. In December a parliamentary panel called for the government to finalize its recognition of the university’s accreditation and widely replicate its model of project-based learning and “Indian Knowledge Systems” throughout the country.

That model cannot be scaled up too soon. More than half of Indians are under the age of thirty, and more and more of them can’t find work. Youth unemployment for those aged fifteen to twenty-nine has climbed to over 15 percent; last year a think tank estimated that 44 percent of Indians in the twenty-to-twenty-four age bracket were unemployed. Graduates emerging into this stagnant job market are left to vent online, echoing the frustrations around corruption and reservation of government jobs for elites and high-caste groups that triggered the recent Gen Z revolts in Bangladesh and Nepal.

Despair and anger are spreading among the swelling ranks of college graduates who see the promised path to a middle-class life—a stable, salaried job—turning into a mirage. More and more find themselves grinding away as wage laborers or delivery workers in the choking pollution of cities like New Delhi. Some seek opportunities in the gig economy; some, failing to find work at all, return home to toil on village farms. Their precarity is increasingly compounded by the climate crisis: about 90 percent of India’s workers are in the informal sector, operating or working for small, unincorporated businesses or performing agricultural or casual labor, and three quarters of the nation’s workforce are exposed to extreme heat in their daily exertions. India’s current student ferment differs in important ways from the chaotic uprising against nepotism and corruption that burned through Nepal in 2025, or the youth-led revolution that ended the fifteen-year rule of Sheikh Hasina in Bangladesh in 2024. But as Ashok Swain, an expert on resource conflict, wrote recently, there is one common thread linking the recent youth-led uprisings across the region: “South Asia’s youth, digitally connected and politically alienated, are no longer willing to wait passively for better governance.”

The catalyzing event for India’s swelling tide of youth protest came in May, when officials suddenly canceled nationwide medical college entrance exams because the questions were leaked in advance. (This is a recurring issue that the education ministry has done little to fix: since 2014, there have been at least 152 leaks of national entrance exam questions.) The decision, which nullified the test results of 2.2 million students, triggered widespread fury. The pressure to pass these rigorous exams, and become the one in seventeen who secure a spot in medical schools, can be overwhelming. Some poorer families sell off land and take on heavy debt to finance their children’s studies and preparation for the exam, even as those with wealth and connections conspire to purchase leaked questions from corrupt officials. At least a dozen students committed suicide in the wake of the cancellation.

On May 15 another spark was lit when the chief justice of India’s Supreme Court compared unemployed youths to “cockroaches” and “parasites.” The next morning Abhijeet Dipke, a thirty-year-old Indian graduate student in Boston, posted half-jokingly on social media: “What if all cockroaches came together?” Within days, satirical online memes about forming a “Cockroach Janta Party” had morphed into an actual movement, catalyzing large protests in major cities. In June CJP leaders began calling for accountability and an overhaul of the education and examination system. Wangchuk, whose own rhetorical style often marries outward playfulness with a deep seriousness of purpose, praised how creatively the organizers had channeled their rage into humor, and advised the government to listen to them; in the lead-up to his fast on the students’ behalf, he dubbed himself an “honorary cockroach.”

Ladakh sits on the bleeding edge of both the country’s joblessness crisis and of its climate breakdown. The unemployment rate for young graduates is triple the national average. Ever since Modi cleaved the state of Jammu and Kashmir into two union territories seven years ago, more graduates are competing for ever fewer jobs: in July 2025 the Ladakh UT administration received more than 50,000 applications for 534 vacant positions. Young Ladakhis describe being trapped in a sclerotic system designed to prepare them for jobs that don’t exist. Their criticisms, in recent years, of an unresponsive local administration that promises recruitment and exams only to cancel them without explanation prefigured the admonitions of the CJP protesters thronging the nation’s capital in recent weeks.

The youth of Ladakh are also acutely aware of a still larger crisis: the region’s geography makes it distinctly vulnerable to the rapid climatic changes India is experiencing. While most Indians are exposed to the vagaries of the monsoon, Ladakhis live in the “rain shadow” cast by the Himalayan range. With little rainfall to sustain them, they secure nearly all their water from snow and ice-melt; some Ladakhis can glance up at the mountaintops, gauge how much frozen water they hold, and calculate how many rows of crops they will be able to irrigate in a given year. Over the past few decades, Ladakhis have watched as warmer winters and erratic snowfall turn summer irrigation flows into trickles and village springs dry up. Once-mighty glaciers are vanishing before their eyes. In many villages, farmers run out of water to irrigate their fields of barley and peas and alfalfa by midsummer. Some communities have abandoned their lands due to worsening drought.

Wangchuk has tirelessly called attention to this existential threat. The ratcheting loss of Himalayan ice and snow, he always stresses, has downstream consequences that are impossible to overstate. “It’s the largest reservoir of fresh water outside of the poles, feeding one fourth of the planet’s population, directly or indirectly,” he told me in 2024. “It’s not just Ladakh’s problem. It’s everybody’s problem.” In another conversation the year before, while he was preparing to fast atop the 17,582-foot Khardung La in midwinter (a protest the authorities ultimately forbade him from undertaking), he explained his motivation: “In Ladakh, we are in a very important position to be messengers from the frontier…. We have a responsibility to tell the world what’s happening with us today, because tomorrow it will be happening to you.”

Indian officialdom has long viewed Ladakh through a very different lens—as a “sensitive border region” to secure. Ladakh is surrounded by territory controlled by India’s adversaries China and Pakistan, which have a strategic alliance, and India has long been anxious to maintain military access, in the event of hostilities, to its disputed borders—both the “Line of Control” to the west that divides Indian- from Pakistani-controlled Kashmir, and the “Line of Actual Control” to the east, which loosely demarcates territory respectively controlled by India and China since their 1962 war. Over the past few decades the government’s road-building agency has been clawing away at deep gorge walls and 15,000-foot passes to build a suite of year-round, all-weather roads for moving battalions and materiel.

Then, in 2019, came Modi’s announcement that he was abrogating Article 370 of India’s constitution—the provision that provided Jammu and Kashmir with special status—and breaking the state into two distinct union territories to be ruled directly from New Delhi. It was lost on no one that Modi chose to unilaterally dissolve the only Muslim-majority state in the country, stripping it of its state constitution and eliminating the provisions that had restricted nonresidents from owning land within its borders. In Kashmir the government imposed a prolonged Internet shutdown, clamped down on the media, and arrested hundreds of Kashmiri politicians and thousands of young protesters.

Ladakhi Buddhists, for their part, had long agitated to be free of what many viewed as neglect and unfair treatment by Kashmiri leaders in Srinagar, and most of them, including Wangchuk, initially welcomed the arrival of union territory status. But they soon experienced some buyer’s remorse when they realized that the BJP’s leaders intended to curtail rather than expand avenues for local democracy. After Article 370 was abrogated, Ladakhi Buddhists and Muslims alike suddenly found themselves without substantive legislative powers. The autonomous hill development council was rendered largely impotent, its administrative and financial authority—including over crucial land use policies—siphoned away by New Delhi and handed to its appointed lieutenant governor.

Since then, mining firms have begun scouting the region’s abundant limestone, silica, borax, and other mineral deposits; luxury hotel chains are starting to enter the local market; and the central government, with minimal local input, has begun work on a massive thirteen-gigawatt solar and energy project in the high-altitude plains of eastern Ladakh, along with a 713-kilometer high-voltage transmission line to Haryana. Ladakhis are broadly supportive of solar energy—solar panels and solar water heaters have adorned rooftops in the sun-drenched region for decades. But unease is spreading about the lack of safeguards to ensure that the project’s benefits flow to locals, and some of the region’s semi-nomadic Changpa herders fear that the development will shut them and their pashmina goats out of ancestral grazing lands.

A year after Modi dismantled the region’s constitutional guardrails, another event accelerated the government’s own building spree in Ladakh. In June 2020 Indian and Chinese troops came to blows along an icy, high-altitude section of the LAC. They brawled with bare hands, spiked clubs, and rocks. Twenty Indian soldiers and an undisclosed number of Chinese soldiers were killed. The skirmish dredged up the humiliation of India’s defeat in 1962, when the People’s Liberation Army occupied the Aksai Chin territory, thereby biting off roughly a third of what India viewed as Ladakh’s full land area, which China controls to this day. It also reignited longstanding fears among the political and security establishment in New Delhi that Ladakh’s borders weren’t adequately defended. The imperative of controlling strategic military routes—as well as planned new infrastructure with security implications, such as mineral resource extraction and energy projects—superseded any campaign promises the BJP had made to the region’s inhabitants.

The incident also called attention to the patriotism of Ladakhis, many of whom serve in the army’s storied Ladakh Scouts high-altitude warfare division. Ladakhis turned out in large numbers to greet the bodies of fallen soldiers as they passed through Leh. Wangchuk was no exception to this pattern of patriotic display: after the incident he led a campaign to ban TikTok and other Chinese apps and Chinese-made goods. But he persisted in reminding his audiences in India that border incursions pale in comparison to the existential threat of global warming. “In the face of climate change, armies look like children fighting,” he has said. “I think it is like two neighbors fighting over a fence, when a tsunami is coming very close.”

Wangchuk’s fight to secure Ladakh’s autonomy over its own natural resources, and alert the world to their fragility, has taken him to extreme lengths. In 2022 he bicycled up Khardung La, one of the world’s highest motorable passes, cut out a chunk of ice from its dying glacier, and delivered it to the Dalai Lama in Dharamsala just in time for an Earth Day symposium.

A year later, in January 2023, he announced a five-day “climate fast” atop the 17,582-foot pass, not far from that shrinking glacier; authorities denied him access, forcing him to do it in Leh instead. In March 2024 Wangchuk, along with many other Ladakhis, undertook another fast outdoors in the Himalayan winter to protect what he described as “this sacred water reservoir of the nation.” This one lasted twenty-one days, because that was the longest fast undertaken by Mahatma Gandhi during India’s independence struggle.

That September he and a handful of supporters walked a thousand kilometers across the Himalaya to New Delhi, shuffling on blistered feet all the way from the nation’s “restive border region” to its power center, seeking to pressure Modi and his powerful deputy, Home Minister Amit Shah, to respond to Ladakhis’ demands. Instead authorities detained Wangchuk on the outskirts of the city, on October 1, a day before Gandhi’s birthday—the day he was slated to arrive and pay his respects at Raj Ghat, where an eternal flame burns in Gandhi’s memory. When he was released he began another indefinite fast. After fifteen days the home ministry agreed to hold further talks with the LAB and KDA about their demands; ensuing negotiations in December yielded little beyond desultory offers to reserve a higher share of government jobs for locals. Throughout further talks in January and May 2025, the government refused to budge on statehood and the Sixth Schedule.

At a time when Gandhi’s methods within India and moral appeals to climate action worldwide seem on the wane, Wangchuk is unabashedly pursuing both. He has effectively used tactics like padyatra (long marches) and anshan (fasts) to push Ladakh’s demands to the top of news feeds and political agendas. (There is a certain aptness in the fact that it is an alliance of Buddhists and Shia Muslims, in what was formerly a Sunni-majority state in a Hindu-majority nation, that can lay a credible claim to being the current standard bearer of Gandhi’s message.) During his twelve years in power, Modi’s strongman persona and Hindu-first agenda has crowded out Gandhi’s emphasis on strength-through-nonviolence and inclusive secularism from popular discourse (and even from history textbooks). Gandhi’s broader legacy, meanwhile, has in recent decades come in for criticism from many quarters, most notably for his reluctance to fully denounce the caste system and seek full democratic representation for Dalits, and for some of his regressive, misogynistic views on women’s role in society. But Wangchuk and other Ladakhi activists have succeeded in reminding their fellow citizens of the timeless potency of both satyagraha and cross-sectarian alliances. “We in Ladakh have no choice,” Wangchuk told me. “They can crush anything but Gandhian [resistance] very easily. We have become a nuisance…because of the Gandhian way, and the support that garners from the nation and beyond.”

Here, as ever, his approach has been fundamentally pedagogical. Over the years Modi has often claimed that India has become vishwaguru—a Sanskrit term meaning “Teacher of the World”—under the BJP’s rule. Lately Wangchuk has been offering winking responses, repurposing the prime minister’s rhetoric for quite different ends. “India can become a vishwaguru by promoting Ladakh as a sustainable alternative, rather than repeating the mistakes that ruined places like Bangkok or Goa,” he said in a recent interview. “You become vishwaguru not by what you do in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata,” he elaborated to me, “but [through upholding] indigenous knowledge systems in forests and mountains where tribals live, by creating an harmonious governance system which respects nature, future and culture.”

Behind these cheeky ripostes is a sincere call to pursue moral leadership in the world’s eyes not by promoting Modi’s brand of “yoga and ayurveda diplomacy” but by returning to Gandhian principles like swaraj (“self-government”) and swadeshi (“self-sufficiency”) and respecting India’s dizzying diversity of indigenous, ethnic, and linguistic knowledge. Such appeals are, Wangchuk knows, likely to fall on deaf ears among the country’s current ruling class. But he pitches his rhetorical frequency to reach the antennae of the nation’s media and its youth—the nation’s future leaders.

Those future leaders will have some strong tailwinds behind them, if they decide to take his counsel seriously. Analysts at the think tank Ember recently noted that India is taking a much shorter “detour” into fossil-fueled growth than any other major country in history, electrifying its economy and producing more solar electricity than China did at a similar point in its GDP-per-capita trajectory. This arguably has less to do with particular policies enacted in India than it does with those pursued by China, which have enabled the rapid drop in the cost of solar panels and batteries and the widening availability of affordable electric vehicles. It also owes something to the fact that India’s economy depends more heavily on services and relies less than China does on carbon-intensive industries and construction.

Still, India remains acutely vulnerable to supply shocks like the one triggered by the US war on Iran: imports account for 90 percent of the oil and half of the natural gas the nation consumes. In recent months Indian business leaders and analysts have called on policymakers to speed up the electrification of transportation, deploy more batteries to bolster the country’s creaking grid, and power more manufacturing with solar and super-efficient heat pumps instead of fossil fuels. Last month the BJP chief minister of Delhi announced an aggressive set of new policies to spur adoption of electric two-wheeled and three-wheeled vehicles, including a looming ban on new gasoline- and natural gas-fueled scooters, motorbikes, and autorickshaws, which make up the vast majority of the city’s vehicle fleet. This future, too, was one that Wangchuk rehearsed decades ago. I have a vivid memory of watching him test-drive a solar-powered bicycle rickshaw assembled by students at SECMOL in May 2005. The brakes weren’t yet finished, but that didn’t stop him from pedaling furiously up the dirt road toward Leh, grinning into the morning sun.

Even before Wangchuk’s arrest in September 2025, Modi’s administration had taken steps to punish him for his statehood advocacy. In August of that year the government-controlled local administrators cancelled the land lease of HIAL on dubious grounds. They also revoked SECMOL’s license to receive foreign contributions and announced investigations into its finances. The organization continues its core work of educating teenagers from villages across Ladakh, although it has had to curtail some of its programs that rely on international volunteers.

But Wangchuk’s detention under the National Security Act was a particularly unsettling escalation. It seemed intended to signal how far the government was willing to go in meeting peaceful dissent with the full force of state repression; some commentators described it as a test of India’s democracy and constitutional order. For his part, Wangchuk interpreted his imprisonment as an attempt to “silence my voice for raising the rightful demands of the people of Ladakh.”  

After the clashes of September 24, BJP officials argued that detaining Wangchuk had been effective, since, after all, things had been quiet in Ladakh since. But many Ladakhis reported that their silence was driven by fear. Authorities imposed curfews, banned gatherings of more than five people, and restricted Internet and cell phone use immediately after the riots. Within a few weeks these measures were relaxed, but the chilling effect remained. “Most of the people are angry.… Still we can’t do anything,” a Ladakhi friend told me in February. “Internet is working but we can’t do any protests or rallies. There are more police than before.… We can’t speak against the government.”

Given the skeptical response of the Supreme Court justices to its arguments, it is not exactly surprising that the government, in the end, decided to release Wangchuk in March. When I spoke with him two months later, not long before he commenced his most recent hunger strike, he told me that he remains committed to Ladakh’s statehood movement, but hopes to eventually hand over leadership to “safe hands,” so he can return to focusing on his education work. And yet he remains involved in the ongoing negotiations between Ladakhis and the BJP-led government.

On May 22 Wangchuk and other Ladakhi leaders met with representatives of the home ministry in New Delhi and emerged, they said, with an “in-principle understanding.” Ladakh would not be granted Sixth-Schedule status, but it would get protections similar to those applied to the northeastern states of Sikkim and Nagaland under different articles of India’s constitution. The most important concession was a pledge that Ladakhis would have an elected legislature and a chief minister with real executive powers, shifting authority away from Delhi-appointed bureaucrats—although the memorandum was vague on just what those executive powers would entail.

The announcement met with a positive response in Ladakh, Wangchuk said, even though most Ladakhis are wary of putting their faith in mere promises, having been spurned by the BJP’s leaders again and again. If the BJP follows through, the deal would, paradoxically, bring Ladakhis more tightly into the national fold by trusting them with the power to manage their own affairs and shape their own future in the shadow of those fast-melting glaciers. On July 3 the home ministry confirmed its support for a union territory–level elected body for Ladakh—an encouraging step toward that less precarious, more autonomous future.

By then Wangchuk had begun his recent hunger strike at Jantar Mantar, on a day when temperatures reached 107 degrees in New Delhi. He vowed to fast indefinitely; over the next twenty-six days, he consumed only water and salt. By July 21 he had lost more than twenty pounds. That week heavy rains hammered the mountains of northern India. In Assam, in the northeast, at least seventy-five people were killed and 700,000 displaced by extreme rainfall. In Jammu and Kashmir twenty-seven people were killed by landslides and rising waters. Downpours closed roads, swept away vehicles, and destroyed homes and farm fields in Kargil and other parts of western Ladakh.

Wangchuk finally broke the fast early on Friday, July 24, in the hospital, taking a bowl of soup offered by BJP ministers who had given written assurances that the government wouldn’t take legal action against the young protesters and that their demands for education reforms would be taken up and considered during the current session of Parliament. (The fact that Wangchuk broke his fast with BJP ministers would inspire some backlash in the days that followed; he later explained that CJP and opposition MPs hadn’t been allowed to enter the hospital to be present, despite his request. “Ending a fast in the presence of ministers,” he later told the media, should be “regarded as a symbol of victory.”) Soon after, Modi posted a remarkably solicitous message on X to the man whom his government had imprisoned just a few months earlier: “I urge Sonam ji to follow his routine as per the doctors’ advice and regain his old weight as soon as possible. I pray to the Lord that Sonam ji remains healthy.”

Two days later, the embattled education minister resigned. As the thousands of young protesters still assembled at Jantar Mantar celebrated, reveling in their newly discovered influence on India’s political trajectory, Wangchuk—still wearing his hospital gown, being monitored by doctors nearby—congratulated them in an online post: “IT’S A VICTORY OF DEMOCRACY… direct democracy… straight from the streets,” he wrote. “FROM ACCOUNTABILITY, NOW TO REFORMS.” He was discharged on July 27, and paid a solemn visit to Raj Ghat before heading home to Ladakh.

entries.title: Homer vs. Hollywood: Daniel Mendelsohn on Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey
entries.summary: In this special hour-long edition of NYRSeminars, Daniel Mendelsohn, Editor-at-Large of The New York Review and author of the most recent translation of Homer’s epic, discusses Christopher Nolan’s polarizing blockbuster adaptation of the Odyssey.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this special hour-long edition of NYRSeminars recorded July 29, 2026, Daniel Mendelsohn, Editor-at-Large of The New York Review and author of the most recent translation of Homer’s epic, discusses Christopher Nolan’s polarizing blockbuster adaptation of the Odyssey. Mendelsohn outlines his judgment of the film, which he reviewed at length for the Review, and then opens the floor to questions from audience members. Among the topics addressed are the debate over the fidelity of the film’s sets, ships, and costumes; the film’s handling of its female characters; and the question of whether the director’s vision of Odysseus represents a betrayal of the epic’s values.

For a limited time, we are offering a special 25% discount code toward purchase of the recordings of Mendelsohn’s six-part Odyssey seminar as well as his classics-related books Three Rings, Ecstasy and Terror, and Waiting for the Barbarians, published by New York Review Books. Use the links above or the code “odysseyevent” at checkout in our shops to receive the discount.

About Daniel Mendelsohn

Daniel Mendelsohn is an award-winning author, critic, essayist, and translator. His eleven books include the international bestsellers An Odyssey: A Father, a Son, and an Epic and The Lost: A Search for Six of Six Million; a translation, with commentary, of the Modern Greek poet Constantine Cavafy; and three collections of essays, most recently Ecstasy and Terror: From the Greeks to Game of Thrones (2018). Over the past thirty years. Mr. Mendelsohn has contributed over three hundred essays, reviews, articles, and translations to numerous publications, most frequently The New Yorker and The New York Review of Books, where he is Editor-at-Large, and has been a columnist for The New York Times Book Review, New York magazine, and BBC Culture. His writing for mainstream publications covers a wide range of subjects, from Classical civilization to contemporary literature, as well as film, theater, opera, and television. Mr. Mendelsohn’s honors include the National Jewish Book Award, the National Book Critics’ Circle Award, the American Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Prose Style, the Society for Classical Studies Presidents’ Medal, Princeton University’s James Madison Medal, the Prix Médicis in France and the Malaparte Prize in Italy, that country’s highest literary honor for foreign authors. In 2022, he was made a Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters by the Republic of France. Since 2019, he has been the director of the Robert B. Silvers Foundation, a charitable trust that supports writers of nonfiction, essay, and criticism.

Daniel Mendelsohn, the Charles Ranlett Flint professor of Humanities at Bard College, lives in the Hudson Valley of New York. His translation of Homer’s Odyssey was published by the University of Chicago Press in Spring 2025.

entries.title: A Taste of Infinity
entries.summary: With his commitment to impractical and borderline impossible projects, the composer Dylan Mattingly has created a welcoming, abundant, sun-drenched musical landscape.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Practical advice can be bad for the soul of an artist. And if you happen to be a composer of orchestral music or operas, you have chosen the most impractical of professions: the art you practice is among the world’s least commercially viable. You surely ended up on this path that is no path because early in life you had a transformative experience with music by some artist who impractically, improbably managed to create a transcendent communal experience out of pure sound.

And yet, throughout your years of musical training, you will be beset by reasonable, well-intentioned, utterly depressing advice that, if you heed it, will deflate your artistry and make your music sad and small. Every composer has encountered this kind of counsel, which can metamorphose into an insidiously persuasive inner voice: Make sure you write a nice short orchestral piece as a calling card. You know, a quick little fanfare, the kind of thing that’ll get played a lot, that can be squeezed in before the concerto in the first half of a concert. See if you can give it a topical title. Don’t make it too hard. Don’t make it too dissonant—but careful, don’t make it thoroughly consonant either. Come to think of it, don’t make it too anything.

Among my composer colleagues, one of the few who has steadfastly refused to heed this terrible little voice is Dylan Mattingly, whose career might be thought of as a radical experiment in doing precisely the opposite of what would help a young composer secure a footing in the world of contemporary music. Mattingly, who was born in 1991, spent much of his twenties at work on a single six-hour music theater piece called Stranger Love, which he completed in 2017 but which was not performed in its entirety until 2023. His follow-up to that piece was another six-hour work, titled History of Life. The ludicrous scale of his music and the intense demands it places on musicians ensure that Mattingly sightings on concert programs remain infrequent.

And yet I think that his commitment to impractical and borderline impossible projects has proved more than worthwhile. He has summoned into being a region of musical experience that’s all his own, a welcoming, abundant, sun-drenched landscape that teems with tinkling, deliriously retuned pianos and raucous grooves that last long enough to offer a taste of infinity. A new album called The Wild Heart offers a slice—though admittedly only a small, frustratingly incomplete sampling—of this Whitmanic artist’s fertile, dazzling world within the world.

Stranger Love could be thought of as an opera, though even that all-embracing term feels insufficient for its scope. It might be more accurate to say it’s an opera, a ballet, and a utopian symphonic work wrapped into one. The piece features a libretto by Thomas Bartscherer; its concept is jointly credited to him and Mattingly. The full work has been performed only once, on May 20, 2023, at Los Angeles’s Walt Disney Concert Hall, in a production directed by Lileana Blain-Cruz. Though that performance was produced (and the work commissioned) by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the ensemble that performed, indefatigably, was Contemporaneous, the new-music group that Mattingly helped found as a student at Bard. His cofounder, David Bloom, conducted with the practically superhuman energy, precision, and generosity of spirit that the work demands.*

That performance of Stranger Love remains one of the three or four happiest experiences I have ever had in a concert hall. It prompted an ecstasy comparable to the sensation I had at fifteen seeing Radiohead live for the first time. Mattingly’s achievement might be even more impressive than that of Thom Yorke & Co., since those neurons of total, self-nullifying musical pleasure don’t fire as readily in my thirties as they did when I was a teenager.

Stranger Love’s singular form is inextricable from its beautiful title: the protagonist of the piece is love itself, and the music traces love’s orbit as it widens and grows ever stranger. It is organized in three acts: in the first, we follow a young couple, Tasha and Andre, through a cycle of the seasons, from one spring to the next. Their love blooms in spring, thrives in summer, and encounters threats—doubts, temptations, distance—throughout autumn and winter, before beginning the cycle anew with the “jubilee” of a second spring.

So far, the piece might as well be called Tasha and Andre, but Act Two makes clear that we’re not only following the shared arc of two human lives; we’re following love’s pathways beyond the boundaries of a human relationship, and in this audacious act, love’s orbit unhitches from the human vessels we thought were the main characters. We witness the course of another year, another cycle of the seasons, this time from a more-than-human perspective: Tasha and Andre are absent; the music is mostly instrumental, with occasional wordless contributions from a small vocal ensemble; and the singers are replaced onstage by three pairs of dancers.

Advertisement

In the third act the perspective widens even further: the music is entirely instrumental, and there are no human characters onstage, only (per the creators’ instructions in the score) “a constellation of lights scattered throughout” the performing space. Whatever force is carrying us on its shoulders, this friend or stranger called love, its orbit has enlarged beyond earth’s gravitational field. We seem to be witnessing the love of one shooting star for another.

The acts grow shorter as they expand outward: the first act lasts almost four hours, the second an hour and a quarter, and the third, which sounds as if it were written in a single burst of euphoria, just over twenty minutes. Each act is also arguably written in a different genre: the first act, with its named characters, its sung lines of text, and its traceable storyline, is recognizably an opera; the second act is a kind of ballet; and the third is a symphonic movement, a new ode to joy. We progress steadily from the messy human realm of opera through the increased abstraction of dance into the still more abstracted space of instrumental music, each act and each musical form depicting or enacting love in a new incarnation. Mattingly and Bartscherer have acknowledged Plato’s Symposium as a guiding influence: the first act corresponds to Alcibiades’ speech about love “in a human and personal frame,” the second has a relationship to Aristophanes’ “archetypal account of human love,” and the third is inspired by the vision of divine love that Socrates attributes to the priestess Diotima.

The creators’ inspiration might be Platonic, but their form is recognizably Dantean: a three-part journey from the human realm to a divine one. Dante ends each of the Divina Commedia’s three canticles with a reference to the stars, and Mattingly has a habit of describing his work the same way: he has called the piece “an ecstatic, impossible celebration of being alive that lasts forever and ends in the stars.”

Dante’s spiral moves upward and is pitilessly hierarchical: the pilgrim’s earlier states of being are disavowed and revealed to be both incomplete and full of sin as he ascends toward supreme beatitude. Mattingly’s love supreme, by contrast, seems to move not upward but outward, toward some unimaginable horizon. Like Dante, he moves from a human frame to an unframable cosmic viewpoint, but his tone is gentler and more democratic. The euphoria of Stranger Love’s third act is not so different from the joy those humble humans experience in Act One: there is a kinship between the giddy, tinkling vibrations that open the piece and the ones that conclude it. The camera has panned to an inconceivably wide angle, and yet by the end, despite the inconceivably wide angle, the human world has not been dismissed or negated.

The work’s form-breaking form could be sustained and made bearable to experience only by Mattingly’s exceptionally beautiful music. The tingling, luminous texture depends on the composer’s use of three pianos, each of which is tuned differently from the others. One is in standard tuning (that is, A440 or A442), another is detuned by a quarter-tone (fifty cents), and a third is tuned down by an even smaller interval, just thirty-one cents. You don’t need to understand the physics of it to enjoy this three-headed keyboard creature’s gleeful shimmer, an effect not of dissonance but of abundance and depth, an embodiment of the possible coexistence of multiple ways of being. It is a cosmic arcade piano, one that sounds like an early Bruce Springsteen song blasting out across a boardwalk and heard from a couple of piers away, the sound gently warped by the warm evening breeze. This is a sound that brims with hope, but it’s also full of distance: the sound of a piano ricocheting off a differently tuned one, then another, seems to be the sound of a single piano calling out across time and space, across generations. This nostalgic distance is constitutive of the sound’s texture and is required to sustain its sense of hopefulness.

Throughout Stranger Love, other musicians—singers, string and wind players—are sometimes asked to bend their pitches in similar ways; at such moments, the ensemble becomes a cheerfully squawking or squabbling ecosystem of sound. The other day I walked by a field and noticed that the intonation of several birds in different trees, peaceably coexisting but each sticking to its own tune, varied by roughly the same micro-intervals as Stranger Love’s pianos.

Mattingly’s work recognizably emerges from multiple strands of American minimalism: Stranger Love contains affectionate nods to Meredith Monk’s lunar syllablescapes and the wild-eyed, gleefully scraggly sixteenth notes of John Adams’s Shaker Loops (1978). But something in me revolts at the notion of associating the word “minimal” with music of such teeming superabundance. Mattingly frequently crafts soundscapes of rhythmic and textural intricacy that are nonetheless fairly stable harmonically. This sets him apart from past minimalists. Many commentators have noted that Adams’s music, starting in roughly the late 1980s, became more complex, by which they generally mean more harmonically varied and less dependent on repetitive rhythmic structures. What’s notable about Mattingly’s music is that he frequently forges textures of dizzying complexity within repetitive rhythmic structures and relative harmonic stasis.

Composers who write operas often face pressure from commissioners to imitate the breathless pacing of a Broadway show; there’s a widespread fear that if the onslaught of event after event ever flags, a new opera might lose the attention of the least engaged, most distracted members of its audience. Mattingly understands, though, that temporal dilation is one of the most potent tools an opera composer can wield and that many of the most cherished moments in the history of the form derive their power from a steady gathering of energy in the preceding minutes or hours. (Think of the brass-crested waves at the end of Richard Wagner’s Das Rheingold, which finally break after having stealthily accumulated across nearly three hours.) Sometimes in music, a great expanse of time is required to give full expression to a sensation that in life might last just an instant. In the third scene of Stranger Love’s first act, Tasha and Andre realize that they are helplessly in love. Mattingly summons the vertiginous, falling sensation of new love with a whirling, circular motion in winds, pitched percussion, and his celestial honky-tonk trio of retuned pianistic Muses. This music summons the sensation of being stuck on a merry-go-round that’s spinning too fast after you’ve eaten too much cotton candy, and the composer, mercilessly and correctly, keeps his foot on the gas for an extended duration.

Later in the piece, Mattingly takes audacious risks of pacing in sections of both extreme density and extreme sparseness. There are shockingly lengthy passages of great velocity and rhythmic intricacy, the kind of music that’s delicious to listen to but that might reduce even hardened new-music performers to tears. In the “Spring” section of Act Two, a hilariously difficult passage of vocal hocketing—a ping-pong-like back-and-forth rhythmic pattern passed between singers—is layered across shifting time signatures and repeated for minutes on end. (This seems a little cruel: any rhythmic precision among the singers is likely to disintegrate by the second or third bar.) There are also passages of extended, held-breath stillness. The “Summer” scene of Act Two features more than twenty minutes of languorous, voluptuously dissonant sustained chords in the strings, cut through by the still more pungent plaintiveness of oboe, trumpet, and acutely keening clarinet. It is high summer, we are in a field of tall grasses and choiring insects, and our multifarious protagonist, love, now takes the form of the sun, whose power we experience from the perspective of the field warmed by its inexorable radiance.

The one significant flaw of Stranger Love is the text of the sections spoken in Act One by a narrator called Uriel. I sympathize with the creators’ decision to communicate indispensable narrative information through speech rather than song: Mattingly’s rhapsodic musical idiom possesses no conversational register; there’s no equivalent to the wry tenderness of Mozartean recitative or Kurt Weill’s world-weary Sprechstimme. The trouble is not with the presence of spoken material but with its tone. In the opera’s first scene, Bartscherer’s introduction of the main characters makes them sound pretty insufferable:

We begin at a garden party. Tasha is a novelist who’s had considerable success with her first book. Andre is a theologian and a doctoral candidate known for his dedication to the spirit of skepticism.

Subsequent spoken sections are studded with oddly pedantic references to writers both ancient and modern: Anne Carson, Octavio Paz, Ovid. (“The Latin poet Ovid, who wrote a famous book about love, wrote an even more famous book about how everything changes.”) I admire these artists, but I winced every time they were referenced; even the sound of their names felt intrusive and dissonant, like a piercing rush of feedback from a mic or King Marke bursting in on the lovers’ sanctuary in Tristan und Isolde. Mattingly has created a luminous, self-sufficient musical world, and these fusty if mercifully brief spoken interludes ought to be rewritten so that they no longer break the music’s spell.

At the intermissions of Stranger Love’s one performance, a consensus formed among the Disney Hall concertgoers—the kind of consensus that can’t be trusted, based as it is on a piece’s most obvious qualities as well as on listeners’ desire to find common ground; intermission conversations tend to coagulate into a cautious centrism. In this case, the consensus was: this is a very interesting piece, to be sure, but it’s much too long. I disagreed. When Stranger Love finally reached the other shore of its six-hour odyssey, I yearned for it to keep going.

There are currently no plans for the piece to be performed in public again, and other than brief excerpts, no recording is available. Our world is a mess, and Stranger Love might be too good for it.

What is a composer supposed to do after writing a work whose bonkers ambition rivals the most preposterous acts of opera making in recent history, a work that can be mentioned in the same breath as Karlheinz Stockhausen’s Licht cycle? Some composers might lie fallow for a few years, or they might dash off a few little piano mazurkas, the kind of thing they could hand to a friend and hear performed a month later.

But that’s not Mattingly’s way. In 2017, shortly after putting the final touches on Stranger Love, he and Bartscherer began dreaming up their next musical cosmos, History of Life, another six-hour work of music theater. This piece sets the ambitious goal of weaving the tale of the aged Odysseus’s journey home, the explorations of Charles Darwin, and the story of an adolescent girl on the Cape Verdean island of Santiago in the nineteenth century “into an enormous musical tapestry that comes to encompass the whole bewildering narrative of organic life on Earth.”

Stranger Love has been performed just once, but there hasn’t been even a single complete performance of History of Life. However, Mattingly has quieted his inner completist and created a roughly hour-long suite of music derived from it, which he calls The Transmutation Notebooks; the name comes from the journals in which Darwin sketched his theory of evolution. The Wild Heart includes this suite, together with Sunt Lacrimae Rerum (2020), a piece for two harps and two retuned pianos.

Though the continuity between Stranger Love and these more recent works is instantly apparent—the extended, sunny major-key textures, refreshingly carbonated by unconventionally tuned pianos—there are also subtle differences. A clue to this evolution might be found in Mattingly’s program note of Sunt Lacrimae Rerum, which was composed in the fall of 2020, in the aftermath of “the day the sun never came up” in the San Francisco Bay Area, a day kept chokingly dark by wildfire smoke. Even before those wildfires, 2020 had already been a crushing, airless year, and Mattingly decided that rather than give voice to the world’s all-too-obvious misery, he would seek to write “music for dancing, the barbaric yawp, a scream of joy.”

In one sense, this was nothing new for him: Stranger Love is among the most joyful pieces I know. But the joy of Stranger Love (which was composed between 2012 and 2017) bubbles up, effloresces, blooms into being with perfect naturalness. The music on The Wild Heart, written during the first Trump presidency and the Covid pandemic, bespeaks a different kind of joy, a joy clung to and retrenched into with effortful defiance, a joy that willfully refuses everything that isn’t joy, a joy that verges on desperation.

The phrase “sunt lacrimae rerum” is drawn from the passage in the first book of Virgil’s Aeneid in which Aeneas, newly arrived in Carthage after fleeing the devastated Troy, encounters an artistic depiction (either a painting or a frieze) of the war he has just escaped. His life, already rendered into art, has preceded him. He is intensely moved and breaks into tears as he addresses his friend Achates. This little phrase has confounded and divided translators for centuries, since it contains two ambiguities: “sunt” can mean “there are” or “they are” or “these are,” and “rerum” can mean either “of things” or “for things.” A literal rendering would be something like “these are the tears of things” or “there are tears of things,” but Robert Fagles opted for “the world is a world of tears”; Robert Fitzgerald rendered it “they weep here/For how the world goes,” while John Dryden and other translators ignored the phrase altogether. Pope Francis, however, in an encyclical published the same year that Mattingly wrote Sunt Lacrimae Rerum, summoned these words as an image of the planet’s sorrow at the abuses it has suffered at human hands: “The world is itself crying out in rebellion. We are reminded of the well-known verse of the poet Virgil that evokes the ‘tears of things,’ the misfortunes of life and history.”

Mattingly, unsurprisingly, has a sunnier reading: “These are not tears of sorrow—or at least not sorrow alone. These are the tears of everything, of the everythingness present in each moment.” I read the phrase as Virgil’s quiet aesthetic manifesto, a definition of art itself. Aeneas speaks these words as he observes an artistic rendering of his life, and what he says is that these—the images before him—are the tears of things, the tears of matter. The beautiful implication is that the carvings on a temple or the paint on a cave wall might be the stone’s lachrymal exhalation, a transmutation of matter into a form that, while still material, stands one degree closer to spirit, like a first pressing of olives into oil.

Mattingly’s Sunt Lacrimae Rerum begins with a gentle, twinkling fanfare, like some beneficent monk beaming and bowing as she welcomes us into the piece’s precincts. The music soon leaps into a fast, much-repeated groove that reveals Sunt Lacrimae Rerum to be a gleaming shard cast out of the same fire that forged Stranger Love. The two harps are in standard, equal-temperament tuning, but the two pianos are retuned in subtle, nuanced ways, so—just as in Stranger Love—three separate intonation systems are present at any given moment. This piece, whose composition began in a week with no sun, is a welcome bottling up of sunshine. And thanks to its spare but quintessentially Mattinglyesque instrumentation, it serves as a good introduction for newcomers to his music’s essential materials.

I have caught glimpses of History of Life whenever it’s been possible: a relatively brief excerpt at Roulette, in Brooklyn, in 2022; an outdoor performance of the first act at Kaatsbaan Cultural Park in 2024; and a private performance of selected excerpts last year in New York City. My sense, from these performances as well as the music on The Wild Heart, is that History of Life is a gentler, softer-textured, less aesthetically ambitious and less internally varied work than Stranger Love. It is hugely pleasurable to experience but not overwhelming; it is familiar and comforting rather than revelatory.

Given the rhapsodic, everything-all-at-once language with which Mattingly is inclined to discuss his music, it can be hard to distinguish one piece’s aesthetic aims from another’s. But a close look at Mattingly and Bartscherer’s program note for History of Life reveals noticeable differences from their earlier creation: the later piece is described as

a folk revival, a rock concert, a communal feast, and a meditation on all that has lived and all that has died in this world…. More than just a performance, History of Life is a celebration—like a wedding or a wake.

I think we should take that description at face value. This is celebratory music, music that’s ideally suited for an outdoor festival with campfires blazing and plenty of room for everyone to dance.

The Transmutation Notebooks, the suite derived from History of Life, opens with “Ulysses Dances,” a movement that displays the improbably intense voltage Mattingly can wring from a melody that traverses just three notes. The second movement, “Notes for Another Life,” features a prime example of rhythmic intricacy within harmonic stasis: early on, in a gentle and unambiguous G-major harmony, a harp, two vibraphones, two guitars, and a mandolin divide each 4/4 bar into increments of twelve, fourteen, eleven, eight, ten, and nine respectively; the cumulative effect is a tender, incalculable shimmer. The suite’s highlight might be its third movement, “The History of Life in Reverse,” which fulfills the promise of its title by elaborating a simple, chiming piano figure into ever more infinitesimally detailed textural worlds: we seem to be staring backward through evolution, tracing a folk tune (a few minutes in, by which I mean a few thousand years back, we encounter the bardic thrumming of a Homeric harp) as it steadily dissolves into a musical image of billions of tiny, wriggling aquatic beings, our most distant ancestors. In the movement’s final minutes, we stare into the dazzling, blinding plenitude of the ocean.

In addition to asserting that the piece is, at heart, a kind of rock concert, the creators of History of Life make the grander claim that it “bears witness to the vast, beautiful, violent, many-voiced history of life on Earth.” With this in mind, it’s a little surprising that it seems considerably milder than their previous creation, whose subject was love. In that work, Mattingly thrillingly dared to musicalize even the bleakest incarnations of love’s power: the desolate periods when love seems to be far away, occluded, on the dark side of the moon. But though Mattingly and Bartscherer’s description of History of Life gestures at the reality of violence and suffering, they don’t seem to reckon with much violence, darkness, or difficulty in the piece itself, which feels (based on the substantial portions that I’ve heard) like an admittedly awesome extended jam session. And though they point to life’s polyvocality, the one voice that consistently shines through is Mattingly’s irrepressibly cheerful one; the counterpart to joy, in this work, is not darkness or a confrontation with life’s injustices but rather a gentle, melancholy tenderness. This would be fine in many cases, but it’s a problem in a piece whose title and stated aims could hardly be more capacious.

It might be argued that, just as love is the protagonist of Stranger Love, life itself is the protagonist of History of Life, and that from life’s perspective, the sufferings and deaths of innumerable individual beings aren’t especially painful. This seems, however, like a risky perspective for an artist to assume, one that could easily turn inhumane. When exactly does a relishing of the best of life turn into complacency? When might advocacy for joy tilt into a joy addiction?

But Mattingly has plenty of time to explore once again the full spectrum of human and musical experience. He remains blessedly unwilling to climb into any prefabricated box, and for this reason, his generous, virtuosically impractical work is unlikely to find a regular home—for now—at the world’s opera houses or symphony orchestras. But it is out there for those willing to find it. And Mattingly is one of those rare artists who are willing to forge ahead, then stop somewhere waiting for you.

entries.title: Out of the Rubble
entries.summary: In novels written immediately after World War II, Wolfgang Koeppen mined the conscience of Germany.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Small wonder that Wolfgang Koeppen’s native Germany greeted his suite of postwar novels with hostility when they were first published in the early 1950s: When things go wrong, who needs to be shamed? Who needs to be mocked? Who needs—even worse—to be warned? The past is over, that’s its whole point.

Now that the past of those years—the years immediately following World War II—has been superseded by so many other pasts, these novels are apparently received in Germany with (however temporarily) the great admiration and pleasure that was always their due. My own experience with them, though less illustrative, is vaguely parallel to Germany’s: some decades ago an acquaintance gave me a copy of Death in Rome, the third volume of the so-called postwar trilogy, and urged me to read it. I opened it up, it was opaque and inert, I closed it, and thought no more about it until recently, when it was reissued along with a new translation of Pigeons on the Grass and the first English translation of The Hothouse. Out of mild curiosity, I opened it up again, and, who knows why—possibly the atmospheric conditions of 2026—comets and stars came exploding out. I proceeded to read the three books in sequence, dazzled and enthralled, and every time I put one down (which, owing to their richness, intensity, velocity, and sheer unexpectedness, was often) I wondered what on earth had just happened to me; it seemed I’d been tuned, sharpened, elasticized—reformulated with better neurons.

Pigeons on the Grass is the earliest of the three, published in 1951, followed by The Hothouse in 1953 and Death in Rome in 1954. Koeppen wrote them “live,” as it’s put by Michael Hofmann, whom readers can thank for the remarkable translations—“live” meaning in real time and also in real place, Germany, where Koeppen was born in 1906. His long life is interesting—no doubt easier to read about than to have lived, as you can see from the excellent essays by Hofmann, Pankaj Mishra, and Joshua Cohen included in the volumes.

During the days of the Weimar Republic, Koeppen made a living at this and that, for a while as a journalist, and wrote two well-received and poorly selling novels. In 1933, when Hitler was appointed chancellor and Nazism established as Germany’s sole state power, Koeppen went to Holland. As he was not Jewish, or Roma, Sinti, Black, Slavic, homosexual, a communist, a labor leader, or, formally, a dissident, he was not likely to be in official danger, but his publisher was a Jew, he had Jewish friends, he was by nature an intellectual and an aesthete—a type that autocrats tend to view, understandably, with great distaste. And personal safety aside, who, I ask you, wants to live in a country given over to insane, sadistic, thieving, power- and money-mad psychopaths?

In late 1938, just as droves of distinguished writers, artists, scholars, and scientists were fleeing Germany and its occupied or soon-to-be-occupied territories, Koeppen returned. Hofmann tells us that he “lacked the fame, the contacts,…the aptitude for languages, and perhaps ultimately, the brute necessity required to make a go of things in exile.” He also, clearly, lacked the money that might have compensated for those other deficiencies. In 1939 he flew into Berlin, the seat of Nazi operations, where he warily made a living in the film industry, although, owing to either guile or good luck, few of the projects he worked on were realized. In 1944 the apartment building where he lived was destroyed in an Allied air raid, and he slipped off untraced to Munich. A few years later he married eighteen-year-old Marion Ulrich. The relationship seems to have been turbulent and ardent, and they are buried together. He wrote various things in the forty years between these extraordinary books and his death in 1996, but he published no other fiction. He never had money.

Eccentric in just about every way, this trilogy shares no characters (unless you count an image of Frederick the Great on a broken teacup that makes brief appearances in both Pigeons on the Grass and The Hothouse). Nor do the books share settings—the first takes place entirely in Munich, the second in Bonn, and the third in Rome—nor are their stories related. And they are very different in some ways that seem musical, like key, scoring, tempo.

Koeppen was an insatiable reader, and these books demonstrate his assimilation of early-twentieth-century modernist techniques—stream of consciousness, startling disjunctions, abrupt switching of narrative perspective, typographical oddities, and the like. It’s entirely possible that he methodically aimed for specific effects, but his style, which includes plenty of conventional narration too, feels more like an exuberant ad hoc improvisation than virtuoso display or literary experimentation—a flexibility in pressing circumstances, as someone marooned on a desert island might hurl a shoe, then a tortoise, to get an apple down from a tree instead of waiting for a ship to happen by with an apple-harvesting machine. The prose, at least as it comes to us in Hofmann’s worked magic, is simultaneously wild, fluid, often flat-out gorgeous, and uncannily precise. Reading, one feels at the center of a living thing rather than looking on from a safe distance—receiving thoughts and sensations just as they’re hatching into the articulable.

The fundamental unifying element of the trilogy, though, I’d say, is the simple implicit question: Does something in our nature compel us to repeatedly bring hell upon ourselves? The question is posed within the “live” historical moment in which the books were written, those few years after Germany conceded defeat in 1945, when the terrible war—which killed upward of 70 million, including the millions, mostly Jews, murdered by the Nazis—finally ground to a halt. It was a strange, unfixed interim, quickly eclipsed by the distortions and residues of time, by desperate needs and sudden opportunities, by the simple cinematic appeal of the grotesque objectives and machinery of Nazism, by the dramatic notion of “the end,” which camouflages beginnings, by the human gift for fashioning heroic images out of old junk, and so on. Actually, it was a critical interval—unsettled and unpredictable—an abrupt break in continuity, and like other broken things, it disclosed materials that are usually concealed or contained. These books are, among so much else, a reclamation of that moment of rapidly crystallizing forms in a country that concentrated so many hazardous volatile essences—an alarm, still sounding, as loud as ever, under a turf of ambient noise.

Almost from one day to the next, millions of Germans had awakened from the fever dream of imminent triumph and race-pure world domination to find themselves essentially soaked with incriminating blood, clutching the gnawed bones of their former neighbors. Millions of others, of course, had simply kept their heads down and held their breath through the nightmare their own country had induced. Still others were emerging from the camps of which they were the few starving survivors, or from the European forests, caves, and cemeteries where they had hidden throughout the years of the war. Children, parents, lovers, and friends were dead, murdered, or simply gone; where there had been homes, villages, ancient splendor, there was rubble. The matter of identity was at the forefront: What did yesterday’s passport, nation, history, ethnicity, affiliations mean, and how were they to be dealt with? The printers were busy minting new names and birthdays.

Each of these three novels is complete in itself; they can be read singly or in any order, but there’s something to be said for reading Pigeons on the Grass first, as I did, since it provides a kind of aerial view of that particular moment and of a range of individuals and relationships caught within its circumstances. Even before the cast of characters appears, we are given a quick look at their milieu:

Planes were over the city, birds of ill omen. The noise of their engines was thunder, was hail, was storm. Storm, hail, and thunder, every day, every night, landing and takeoff, death exercises, a hollow roar, a flinch, a tremor of memory in the ruins. For the moment, the bomb bays of the planes were still empty. The soothsayers smiled. No one looked up at the sky.

The next paragraph brings us streaking into terrifyingly familiar headlines:

Oil out of the arteries of earth, stone-oil…deposits of dinosaur lard, lizard carapaces…the buried inheritance guarded by dwarfs, by evil, greedy mages, the mythical devil’s hoard…lugged up to the light of day, it was put to use…. War over Oil, Conflict Escalates…Attack on the Pipeline…Here as there people were stockpiling gunpowder to blow the planet to smithereens, Atom Tests in New Mexico, Atom Plants in the Urals…. They spoke of rebuilding and made plans for demolition.

We are then abruptly redirected from the menace overhead and underground and brewing throughout the abstract world to the surface of the earth, where in the city of Munich humans are enacting for us one day of their human business. They include a shopkeeper; a porter; a celebrity and his pansexual wife; the punitive, sin-obsessed nanny of their terrified little daughter, and the child herself; two serious writers, one a very famous, exquisitely cultivated American poet who lives in England and is visiting Munich to give a much-anticipated talk, the other a German—not at all famous, blocked, frequently entangled in proliferating slapstick coils of rumination and uncertainties; the beautiful young wife of the blocked writer, whose emotional compass is governed by the loss of her enormous pre-war family inheritance; a German secretary formerly employed in the offices of the Wehrmacht and now in the offices of the Black military contingent of the American occupiers; two eleven-year-old boys, one German, one American, both imbued with two generations of their families’ experiences and today engaged in heart-stoppingly tense negotiations over a stray dog; several antique dealers; a German-born Jewish actress who cannot convince her American husband that it would actually not be fun for her to join him on his posting to Munich despite his joyful enthusiasm for the city and its people; a psychiatrist who sells his blood to keep himself afloat; a small tour group of American schoolteachers; a pharmacologically inventive narcolept; and—figuring prominently—two Black American soldiers. Extras and cameos, as in a filmed operetta, include beer drinkers, cooks, prostitutes, priests, fashion designers, children playing, Greek pool sharks, a librarian, rough trade, a jazz band, and party guests. They all have plenty to do; no one is looking up at the sky.
